sections.skill: Use probability and expected value to evaluate premiums, deductibles, and extended warranties

questions.prompt: Each year there is a 2% chance of a $5,000 loss. What is the expected yearly loss?
questions.intro: Expected loss = probability × size of the loss. It is the average loss per year over many people or many years.
sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: The expected loss on a phone is $60 a year, but protection costs $120 a year. What does that suggest?

choices.text: On average, the plan costs more than it pays
The plan is guaranteed to save money every year
The phone is certain to break this year
Insurers lose money on every plan they sell

questions.correct_answer: On average, the plan costs more than it pays
questions.intro: Insurers price premiums above expected losses to cover costs and profit. Buying insurance makes sense for losses you could not afford, not for small ones.
questions.feedback: The $60 gap is the average cost of transferring the risk.
sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: A $40 extended warranty on a $60 blender covers 2 extra years. Which is usually wiser if Ana has an emergency fund?

choices.text: Buy it, because warranties always pay for themselves
Buy two, to double the coverage
Skip it and retain the risk
Return the blender and never buy appliances

questions.correct_answer: Skip it and retain the risk
questions.feedback: The warranty is two-thirds of the price; the loss is small and affordable.
sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: Ana compares deductibles: $500 deductible, premium $1,200; $1,000 deductible, premium $1,050. Which yearly savings come with the higher deductible?
questions.intro: Higher deductibles mean lower premiums. Choose a deductible your emergency fund can cover.
sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: With a 10% chance each year of a claim that would hit the deductible, is the $1,000 deductible (saving $150 a year in premiums, extra $500 cost per claim) a good bet on average?

choices.text: No; it costs about $350 a year more
No; it costs $500 more every year
Yes; it saves about $100 a year
Yes; it saves $650 every year

questions.correct_answer: Yes; it saves about $100 a year
questions.intro: Expected extra cost = probability of a claim × extra deductible. Compare it with the premium savings.
questions.feedback: Expected extra: 0.10 × $500 = $50. Savings $150 − $50 = $100 a year on average.
sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: Out of 1,000 drivers, 30 file a claim in a year. What is the estimated probability of a claim?
questions.intro: Relative frequency estimates probability: events ÷ total.

misconceptions.D: Gives the chance of no claim

sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: Why are premiums usually higher than the expected loss?

choices.text: Insurers do not know the probabilities
Insurers add costs and profit
Expected loss is always zero
The law requires premiums to double losses

questions.feedback: Premiums cover expected claims plus expenses and profit.
sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: An emergency fund makes which choice safer?

choices.text: A higher deductible
Dropping liability insurance entirely
Skipping health coverage
Lowering every policy limit

questions.feedback: Cash on hand can cover a higher deductible.
sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: An insurer covers 10,000 homes. Each has a 1% chance of a $50,000 loss. What total claims should it expect?
questions.intro: Across many policies, actual losses come close to the expected total. This is the law of large numbers.
sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: Why do drivers with past accidents usually pay more?

choices.text: Insurers punish drivers to make an example
Accidents raise everyone's premiums equally
The law sets a fixed fine added to premiums
Their estimated chance of a claim is higher

questions.correct_answer: Their estimated chance of a claim is higher
questions.feedback: Higher expected loss means a higher premium.
sources: NAIC (Consumer insurance guides): Explains auto, home, renters, life, and disability insurance and how deductibles affect premiums. (https://content.naic.org/consumer)

questions.prompt: Why does insurance work better for large groups than for a single person?

choices.text: Losses become predictable on average
Each person's losses become certain
Large groups never have any losses at all
Premiums no longer need to be paid

questions.feedback: With many policies, total losses are predictable even though individual ones are not.
